title: there is/are and have got
tagline: Saying what exists in a place, and what a person or place has.
why: Describing a town, a room or a house — with there is/are and have got — comes up constantly in Listening Part 1 and Speaking Part 2. Mixing the two structures together is the most common A2 mistake, so knowing when to use each one is worth extra marks.

hook.text: Nadia shows a photo. "There's a big lake near my grandma's house, and it's got a little boat." "Wow," says Liam. "Are there any fish in the lake?"
hook.ask: Nadia uses two different structures to describe the lake and the boat. Can you find them both?

diagrams.title: there is/are or have got?

sentences.note: have got = something belongs to / is part of something

diagrams.caption: There is/are talks about a place. Have got talks about a person, animal or place that possesses something.

rows.label: Example
cells: There's a park near my house.
My house has got a garden.

rows.label: Question
cells: Have you got…? / Has she got…?

Positive

use.point: there is/there are: saying what exists

examples.note: there's = there is, for one thing

examples.text: There are two bookshops in the town centre.
examples.note: there are for more than one

examples.text: There isn't a swimming pool at our school.

use.point: some, any and a lot of

examples.text: There are some nice shops on this street.
There aren't any buses after ten o'clock.
examples.note: any, usually in negatives and questions

examples.text: There's a lot of traffic this morning.
There are lots of tourists in Cusco.
examples.note: lots of + plural noun, same meaning as a lot of

use.point: have got and has got: what belongs to someone or something
there is or have got? Don't mix them up

examples.note: one way to say it: the place, then the thing
the other way: the place is the subject

watch_out.wrong: There is two shops on this street.
watch_out.right: There are two shops on this street.
watch_out.why: Use are with plural nouns, not is.

watch_out.wrong: Are there some shops on this street?
watch_out.right: Are there any shops on this street?
watch_out.why: Negatives and questions use any, not some.

watch_out.wrong: My sister have got long hair.
watch_out.why: He/she/it needs has got, not have got.
You always takes have, even in questions — has is only for he/she/it.

watch_out.wrong: There's a lot of tourist in Cusco.
watch_out.right: There are a lot of tourists in Cusco.
watch_out.why: A lot of + plural noun needs the plural form (with -s).

watch_out.right: There's a market in my town. / My town has got a market.
watch_out.why: Don't mix the two structures — choose one pattern per sentence.

l1.es: Hay un parque cerca de mi casa.
l1.wrong: It has a park near my house.
l1.why: Spanish hay = there is/are in English, not it has.

l1.es: Mi hermana tiene el pelo largo.

l1.why: The question needs is/are before there — you can't drop it.

l1.wrong: There isn't some café near here.
l1.right: There isn't a café near here. / There aren't any cafés near here.
l1.why: Some doesn't go in negatives — use a/an (singular) or any (plural).

l1.es: Mi pueblo tiene un mercado grande.
l1.wrong: My town is a big market.
l1.right: My town has got a big market. / There's a big market in my town.
l1.why: Describing what a place has needs have got or there is, not the verb be alone.

remember.trick: THERE IS for a place · HAVE GOT for a person!
remember.tip: Ask: am I saying something exists (there is), or that someone/something owns or includes it (have got)?

dialogue.title: My town, your town
dialogue.context: For a geography project, Sofia and Mateo compare their home towns in front of the class.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Sofia, tell us about your town.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: There's a beautiful main square, and there are two churches.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: No, it hasn't. But there's a big market on Sundays.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: My town has got a beach! There are lots of fishing boats.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Nice! Are there any restaurants near the beach?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Yes, there are a lot of them.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Great descriptions! Has your town got a park too, Mateo?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Yes, it has. There's a small park with a football pitch.

can_do: I can say what exists in a place with there is/are, was/were.
I can use some, any and a lot of/lots of correctly with there is/are.
I can talk about what someone or something has with have got/has got.
summary: There is/are says what exists in a place: There's a park. There are two shops.
Use some in positive sentences and any in negatives and questions.
Have got/has got says what a person, animal or place possesses or includes.
He/she/it needs has got; everyone else needs have got.
A lot of and lots of mean the same thing — don't forget the plural -s on the noun.
